newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia Duma seeks written report on Yeltsin health.
newsitem.headline: Russia Duma seeks written report on Yeltsin health.

text.p: The lower house of the Russian parliament on Friday asked President Boris Yeltsin's doctors to present a written report on his state of health, but failed to muster enough support for a resolution asking him to quit.
A resolution approved by the State Duma by 271 votes to 32 said the Health Ministry and Yeltsin's doctors should present a report by March 1.
Parliament's resolutions on Yeltsin's health are not binding on the president, and the Kremlin has indicated in the past that it sees no need to present a written report on Yeltsin's health.
Only 208 deputies voted for a resolution from communist Viktor Ilyukhin that Yeltsin should quit because he was too ill to govern, not enough to allow the resolution to be passed.
Ilyukhin had also suggested asking the Federation Council upper house of parliament to consider terminating Yeltsin's term because of ill health.
"We are told every day...that Yeltsin's health is satisfactory," Ilyukhin told deputies.
"It is really satisfactory, for a pensioner, but not for the leader of the state. Yeltsin effectively does not rule the state. The country is dying, in the state of deepest crisis..."

Yeltsin, 66, is returning only slowly to the Kremlin after more than seven months of illness. He suffered heart problems for most of the second half of last year and suffered from pneumonia this year.
But the Russian constitution, approved in a 1993 referendum, gives even a sick president strong powers and makes it difficult for parliament to remove him.
Yeltsin said in a radio address on Friday that there was no need to rush to change the constitution.
"Amendments and additions can be made to (the constitution) but you should not rush this. It must be a natural process," Yeltsin said in a six-minute address.

"The constitution is the pivot of the new Russian statehood...It is premature today to subject the new structure of the Russian state, as it is being built, to a test of its durability. It is more than that -- it is foolhardy."
